body.text: I'm S. A couple of years back I was seriously burnt out. I was unaware while it was happening, missing the signs and not recognizing them. That's exactly why this program exists: to help you understand burnout, spot it early, and build tools to manage it. I wish I’d had this program when I needed it.

notes.text: Which of these feel true for you right now?
There's always more to do, and nothing feels finished
I've had communication issues with my manager
I feel energized and look forward to work

body.text: This gives us a first read on how work feels to you day to day. Not everything here is in your control, and that’s alright, because resilience against burnout is something you can build. See you tomorrow.

A thought is a sentence in your head, like "This line is taking forever", whereas a feeling is usually a one-word reaction to that thought, say bored or anxious. Telling them apart helps you see why you reacted the way you did.

For each situation below, one line is a thought, one is a feeling. We have done the first one for you. Frequent power cuts → "They make me furious!" = Feeling; "They make things inconvenient for a lot of us." = Thought

body.text: Good grounding. Tomorrow we start tracking these as they happen day to day.
Burnout clouds your thinking, and tracking it is the first step from being overwhelmed by your thoughts to actually managing them. Two worked examples:
Traffic jam → "This is so frustrating" → irritated.
Deadline approaching → "I won't finish on time" → anxious.

body.text: Now that we have some insights about our real attitude towards work and our real stressors, we’ll explore some activities that will help us improve our relationship with our workplace.

A few years ago I hit a wall. I was juggling research, management, and admin. On top of all that, there were extra roles that didn't even matter to me. I worked harder to force results, but the returns stayed flat. Eventually I realized the effort wasn't worth the cost. Whether you’re a student, a professional, a caregiver or any other role, the lesson remains the same. If the output's plateaued, working harder isn't the fix. Alignment is.

Burnout often comes down to an imbalance between the effort put in and the reward received. Stress only worsens it. Effort might be caregiving, a demanding course, or a job with little tangible payoff. Reward is what you get back, like recovery, a good grade or real recognition.

Welcome back. Burnout often means losing sight of your longer-term goals and values. Write down your personal goals, both long and short term.

For each goal, describe what realistic success looks like. Realistic, not perfect: just genuinely achievable. Example: goal = become a surgeon → realistic success = admission to a solid program, a well-paying job after training. Only list what's genuinely necessary and aligned with your real goals.

body.text: Simple but important. This sets up tomorrow's work on cutting unnecessary load.

Recovering from burnout, it's tempting to overcompensate by taking on even more. The fix: realistically reevaluate what's actually on your plate, lean on your team, and prioritize what's truly urgent.

When you have multiple tasks with different deadlines, tackle what's due soonest first, delegate what doesn't need you directly, postpone what isn't urgent, and break anything large into smaller, shareable pieces.

notes.text: Show two cards side by side(swipe for phone optimization in case it can’t fit a screen)
Analyze a dataset for a meeting scheduled the same day.
Write a report due in a few weeks.
Start with what’s due earliest (in this case, the data analysis).
Delegate tasks that don’t require your direct intervention (have a co-worker handle data collection).
Postpone non-urgent tasks (schedule report writing for later).
If a task is large, break it down into smaller parts and either tackle it yourself or seek assistance (ask someone to help you design and grammar-check the presentation).

options: I can organize my schedule to prioritize the urgent tasks

body.text: We'll build on this over the next couple of days.

We often take on tasks that don't actually help us, like going beyond the call of duty, activities that don't benefit us, things we take on just because we know we can do them. That's often unfair to both you and your colleagues.
Today and tomorrow: go through your non-essential tasks and start shedding them. Postpone, pull out, or delegate. By the day after, aim to have dropped at least some deadweight.

Perfectionism is the need to be, or appear, perfect. While it can drive real excellence, left unchecked it feeds low self-esteem, procrastination, and constant pressure.

Perpetual stress without relief leads to burnout. High standards are fine; the trap is unrealistic standards. Standards which are impossible to hit in the real world. You either burn out chasing the perfect first draft, or you get stuck endlessly "preparing" and never start.

notes.text: What do you think of these sentences?
Show each of these and prompt:
It is good to be a perfectionist some of the time
Being self-critical is a part and parcel of a healthy working style
Sometimes it is good to just start and learn in the process

body.text: We'll go deeper on this tomorrow.

Perfectionism feeds stress and procrastination, and narrows how you see your own work. Nothing ever feels good enough. But perfection is a result of iteration, not a starting point. Example: "I have to write a document for marketing" → perfect outcome: "grammatically flawless, no follow-up questions."

notes.text: Show a sentence and the user has to fill a ‘Perfect Outcome’
I have to write a document for the marketing team. → The document is grammatically excellent, extremely clear and the marketing team has no queries about it.
Show each of these and prompt:

I have to produce content for social media
I have to work on a customer acquisition plan
I am in charge of producing marketing strategy for this product

body.text: Now that we know what we want we’ll work on actually getting it tomorrow.

body.text: With realistic outcomes on the table, tomorrow we work out how to actually get there.

Aim to get things realistically done, not perfectly done. Once there, improve on it. Start beats perfect, every time. Like Nike says, “Just Do It.” Think of realistic goals you’d like to set and steps you can take to achieve them.

notes.text: I have to write a document for the marketing team. → The document is grammatically excellent, extremely clear and the marketing team has no queries about it. → The document had some grammatical errors and the marketing team had a few questions about the document. → The document’s first iteration gets some feedback which is worked upon swiftly. → Create the first draft, double-check it, send it for feedback. Work on the feedback and get approval.
